title: setTimeout and the Task Queue
concept: Even setTimeout(fn, 0) doesn't run immediately. It passes through the Web API into the Task Queue

steps.title: Execute console.log('start')
steps.explanation:
The program starts and the first synchronous line, `console.log('start')`, is added to the call stack and immediately executes.
'start' is printed.

steps.title: Delegating setTimeout
steps.explanation:
When the JS engine encounters `setTimeout`, it delegates the timer setup and the callback function to the browser's Web API.
The JS engine doesn't wait for the timer — it moves on to the next line immediately.

**Analogy**: It's like placing an order at a restaurant (setTimeout), getting a buzzer (callback), and sitting down to do other things (executing the next code) while the kitchen (Web API) prepares your food. The buzzer rings when the food is ready.
steps.keyInsight: The JavaScript engine doesn't count the timer itself — it hands that off to the browser.

steps.title: Execute console.log('end')
steps.explanation:
Because `setTimeout` was handed off to the Web API, the main thread doesn't block — it immediately executes the next synchronous line, `console.log('end')`.
'end' is printed.

steps.title: Execute the Callback
steps.explanation:
Once all synchronous code has run and the call stack is empty, the event loop picks up the `setTimeout` callback from the Task Queue and pushes it onto the call stack.
Only now does `console.log('timeout')` inside the callback execute.
steps.keyInsight: Async callbacks always run after all synchronous code has finished.

quiz.question: What is the output order of setTimeout(() => console.log('A'), 0) and console.log('B')?
options: A → B (setTimeout is 0ms so it goes first)
quiz.explanation:
Even setTimeout(fn, 0) goes through the Web API → Task Queue pipeline.
Only after all synchronous code (console.log('B')) has run does the Task Queue callback execute.

misconceptions.correct:
No.
After 0ms it simply enters the 'Task Queue' — it still has to wait.
misconceptions.why:
**Run-to-Completion**: The event loop cannot push any new work onto the stack until every piece of code currently on the stack has **completely finished**.
Even 0ms means 'later'.

keyTakeaway: setTimeout = registered with Web API → goes to Task Queue when timer fires → runs when call stack is empty
